item.title: Xi to attend APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 09:03:00
CHINA / SOCIETY Xi to attend APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen By Xinhua Published: Nov 13, 2026 09:03 AM
Chinese President Xi Jinping will chair the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting and deliver remarks, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson announced Friday. The meeting will be held in Shenzhen from Nov. 18 to 19 under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," the spokesperson said. The APEC CEO Summit will be held in Shenzhen from Nov. 17 to 18 under the theme "To Prosper and Win the Future Together," the spokesperson said, adding that President Xi will attend the opening ceremony and deliver a keynote speech. President Xi will hold a welcome banquet for participating leaders and representatives, and hold bilateral meetings with foreign leaders on the sidelines of the meeting, the spokesperson added.

item.title: Talent, digital tools playing bigger role in boosting China's rural industries
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 07:58:00
An employee works at an assembly line of China YTO Co., Ltd. in Luoyang, central China's Henan Province, Sept. 8, 2026. (Xinhua/Hao Yuan) China has been strengthening the supporting role of talent and digital tools in rural industrial development as it advances agricultural modernization. In the latest episode of China Economic Roundtable, an all-media talk show hosted by Xinhua News Agency, guests discussed how the country is working to make returning migrant workers and tech-savvy young people a sustainable source of talent for agricultural modernization, and how to further apply digital technologies to farming. In Dongjiao Village in central China's Hubei Province, growing numbers of young migrant workers are returning to their hometowns from cities. The village has been training them in technical skills and business management to help them become a new generation of professional farmers, said Hu Aiguo, the village's Party secretary. The goal is to help more new farmers move from conventional farming to smart farming, Hu said. In Dongjiao, young people who have returned from cities now use smart machinery and sensor networks, and grain growers have formed cooperatives to grow organic rapeseed for premium buyers. "Village development depends on young people putting down roots," Hu said. For Zhao Changbao, director of the Rural Economy Research Center of the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, digital tools are also playing a bigger role in advancing smart farming. "In the past, we farmed largely by watching the sky and the land and relying on experience," Zhao said. "What is changing now is that we are starting to rely on data, algorithms and screens." The change is supported by improvements in rural digital infrastructure. More than 95 percent of China's administrative villages have 5G coverage, and rural internet penetration has reached 69.5 percent. As rural digital infrastructure improves, the share of agricultural production guided by digital information is rising by about 2 percentage points a year in China, Zhao noted. According to this year's "No. 1 central document" -- the first policy statement released by China's central authorities each year and often seen as an indicator of policy priorities -- China will further integrate AI into agricultural development. In September, three government departments jointly unveiled an action plan to promote high-quality development of digital villages. It identifies smart farms, intelligent breeding and AI application scenarios as priorities for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). "Digital villages and AI are no longer optional," Zhao said. "They are essential to agricultural modernization."

item.title: Why becoming a 'gatekeeper' for US protectionism is not in Mexico's interest
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 00:27:00
US Mexico Illustration: Xia Qing/GT Washington has erected a wall of protectionism around the globe, and Mexico is eager to pass it more bricks, helping plug the "loopholes." But the higher this wall rises, the more likely it is to hem in Mexico itself, constraining not only its development prospects but also its independence in shaping trade policy. According to Reuters, Luis Rosendo Gutierrez, Mexico's deputy economy minister for foreign trade, said on Wednesday that the Mexican government had tightened traceability measures with industry to ensure that no steel from China or other countries is rerouted through its territory into the US by exploiting Mexico's trade preferences. Meanwhile, Mexico is urging Washington to ease tariffs on Mexican steel, aluminum and automobiles. Jiang Shixue, a distinguished professor at Hangzhou Normal University, told the Global Times that Mexico's move is rooted in its economic predicament created by strong dependence on the US. Facing US tariff pressure and uncertainty surrounding the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement review, Mexico hopes that aligning itself with Washington's restrictions on trade with China will win concessions from the US. Since 2025, Mexico has repeatedly followed the US to announce measures to impose tariffs on imports from China and other countries without free-trade agreements. It seems that Mexico is actively standing guard at the door on Washington's behalf. While other countries may justify trade barriers as necessary to protect their own industries, Mexico's restrictions appear to be protecting the interests of a "third party." In effect, Mexico risks turning itself into a gatekeeper for Washington's protectionism. This could end up as a potential "Faustian bargain." Mexico hopes to sacrifice part of its economic and trade cooperation with China in exchange for US concessions on tariffs and trade. But it may discover that what it surrenders far outweighs what it could gain. On the one hand, Washington is unlikely to abandon its trade pressure on Mexico. On the other, Mexico risks sacrificing long-term industrial cooperation, supply chain diversification and, ultimately, its economic sovereignty. According to Gutierrez, the country has already reduced steel and aluminum imports from countries including China, South Korea and India, by about 30 percent. Zhou Mi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, pointed out that manufacturing is a pillar of Mexico's economy, and steel and aluminum are essential inputs for industries such as auto manufacturing and machinery. Cutting imports of these materials could further aggravate supply pressures on Mexican manufacturers, disrupting production and undermining supply chain stability. More importantly, if Mexico can readily change its trade policies under external pressure, other countries may begin to question the stability and predictability of its investment and trade environment, he added. Once policy predictability is undermined, the price Mexico pays could go far beyond the immediate costs of tariffs. Just one day before the report, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum stressed that respect for sovereignty and cooperation free from subordination "are non-negotiable" tenets of Mexico's relations with the US. True sovereignty should not be confined to political rhetoric. It should be reflected in a country's ability to independently choose its trading partners, allocate resources according to its development needs and formulate its own economic and trade policies. In an increasingly interconnected global economy, broader international partnerships give countries greater room to maneuver amid external uncertainties. Canada, also deeply integrated into the North American economic system, has not abandoned efforts to diversify its trading partners and is actively seeking to expand cooperation with China and other economies to get rid of its dependence on the US. America's trade wall is America's choice. Mexico has no reason to turn it into its own barrier to development. What Mexico truly needs is not to become another brick in Washington's protectionist wall, but to safeguard its economic sovereignty, preserve its ability to connect with global markets and participate in international industrial chains. Otherwise, in trying to please Washington, Mexico risks cutting off its nose to spite its face.

item.title: Does Taiwan really understand major signals from this commemorative event?: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 00:23:00
A view of the Taiwan Straits is seen from Xiamen port, in East China's Fujian Province. Photo: IC Chinese communists are the most steadfast supporters, loyal collaborators, and faithful successors to the revolutionary cause initiated by Sun Yat-sen. No matter how "Taiwan independence" separatist forces attempt to stir up trouble, historical legitimacy and the moral high ground will always remain firmly with those who steadfastly advance national reunification and national rejuvenation. On the morning of November 12, a gathering commemorating the 160th anniversary of Sun Yat-sen's birth was held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. In his speech at the gathering, Chinese President Xi Jinping called for carrying forward the legacy of Sun, one of the nation's revered revolutionary forefathers, to make joint efforts for national rejuvenation and turn into reality the great dream of all Chinese people since the advent of modern times. Resolving the Taiwan question and achieving the complete reunification of the motherland are hurdles that must be overcome in the process of the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. At this important historical juncture, this high-profile commemoration carries profound contemporary significance and clearly sends extremely important signals. Do all sectors of Taiwan society, especially the island's authorities, get it? For Taiwan, the first signal lies in the significance of commemorating Sun for national reunification. "The spirit of patriotism," "national complete reunification" and "national rejuvenation" stand as inviolable historical orthodoxy and the moral high ground. Sun is a revolutionary forefather revered across the Taiwan Straits. Throughout his life, he traveled far and wide, with "revitalize the Chinese nation" as his most resounding rallying cry, and national reunification as his deepest concern. With remarkable historical foresight, he stated categorically: "Unification is the hope of all Chinese nationals. If China can be unified, all Chinese will enjoy a happy life; if it cannot be unified, they will suffer." This observation profoundly reveals that national unification and the well-being of the entire nation are inextricably bound together. By contrast, the current Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities have engaged in political manipulation through "de-Sinicization" for the sake of partisan interests. While paying lip service to "freedom" and "democracy," they have, in practice, abandoned their historical roots and betrayed their own heritage. This is not only an outright desecration of the shared historical memory of people across the Taiwan Straits, but also a complete betrayal and insult to Sun's lifelong patriotic commitment. Beijing's solemn commemoration of Sun is a major blow against "Taiwan independence" separatist forces and a powerful rebuttal of their distorted view of history, setting the historical record straight. The second signal is to further clarify the mainland's policy stance on peaceful reunification and opposition to separatism under the evolving circumstances across the Taiwan Straits. "Compatriots on both sides of the Taiwan Straits are all Chinese. We are one family bound by blood ties that run deeper than water. As long as family members talk things through calmly and consult each other when issues arise, there are no disputes or differences that cannot be resolved." The political differences between the two sides of the Taiwan Straits are a legacy of history. However, as long as both sides uphold the one-China principle and the 1992 Consensus and sit down for face-to-face communication, there is nothing that cannot be discussed when it comes to the interests, well-being and development opportunities of Taiwan compatriots. Compatriots on both sides of the Straits are one family. Why should they allow themselves to be swayed by the antagonism deliberately stirred up by "Taiwan independence" separatist forces? Why should they allow external forces to turn Taiwan into a pawn in geopolitical rivalry? All sectors in Taiwan should recognize, in particular, that the door to peaceful reunification remains wide open, channels for exchanges and consultations remain accessible, and the interests and sentiments of Taiwan compatriots are given full consideration. They must not allow the DPP authorities' political manipulation in pursuit of "independence" to block the path of cross-Straits communication, much less allow a handful of politicians to hold Taiwan society's future hostage. The dead-end path of "Taiwan independence" separatism has already been firmly blocked. If the DPP authorities persist in seeking "independence by relying on external forces or military means," dragging the residents of Taiwan onto their war chariot, they will inevitably face a harsh reckoning by history and the people. The third signal is that only by adopting a broader historical perspective and an open-minded outlook befitting our times can we see through the layers of confusion, grasp the profound meaning of the principle that "family members should talk things through calmly." In the speech, President Xi highlighted Sun's lifelong devotion to the country, called for emulating, inheriting and carrying forward his invaluable spirit, and called for vigorously promoting the common values of humanity and actively advancing the building of a community with a shared future for humanity. Once we break free from the information cocoons and ideological prejudices created by "Taiwan independence" forces and examine the issue from the broader perspective of the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the profound changes unseen in a century unfolding across the world, the logic becomes unmistakably clear. If humanity as a whole should work together to build a community with a shared future, there is even less reason for compatriots on both sides of the Taiwan Straits, bound by blood ties, to be artificially divided. The grand vision outlined by Sun in Fundamentals of National Reconstruction has not only become reality, but has also grown far richer and more expansive than he originally envisioned. History and reality have repeatedly demonstrated that Chinese communists are the most steadfast supporters, loyal collaborators, and faithful successors to the revolutionary cause initiated by Sun. No matter how "Taiwan independence" separatist forces attempt to stir up trouble, historical legitimacy and the moral high ground will always remain firmly with those who steadfastly advance national reunification and national rejuvenation. We sincerely hope that Taiwan compatriots will recognize the prevailing historical trend, distinguish right from wrong, and join their mainland compatriots in taking concrete action to shoulder the historic responsibility of achieving national reunification and national rejuvenation. The best way to honor Sun is to make the complete reunification of the motherland a reality!

item.title: A newcomer's daily encounters in Brussels reveal how small visual cues turn waste-sorting rules into lasting habits
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 00:09:00
The view of Brussels Photo: VCG During my first week in Brussels, my roommate handed me several rolls of waste bags in different colors. Learning to sort waste, I was reminded, was a basic part of settling in. I would often stand in the kitchen with something to discard in one hand, searching the sorting guide on my phone with the other. Where should a glass bottle go? Which bag should hold a piece of packaging? Even these small decisions required me to check the local instructions again. Before coming to Belgium, I already understood the importance of waste sorting. But with several colored bags in the kitchen, protecting the environment became a succession of practical decisions. Between knowing a principle and performing a small task almost without thinking lies a distance that has to be covered through experience. What information actually helped me take the next step? Looking back, I realized that the guide on my phone, the bags' colors, recycling signs on street corners and my roommate's explanations each played a different part in helping me understand what to do. These unassuming details reveal how communication helps shape everyday habits. A teacher at a kindergarten in Nantong, East China's Jiangsu Province, teaches kids garbage sorting on September 8, 2026. Photo: VCG Colors make sorting knowledge usable In Brussels, yellow bags are for paper and cardboard; blue bags for accepted plastic packaging, metal packaging and drinks cartons; orange bags for designated food waste; green bags for garden waste; and white bags for residual waste. Glass bottles and jars have separate collection arrangements, with clear and colored glass kept apart. For blue bags, "packaging" is crucial: they are not for every plastic item. For a newcomer, the colors initially form a code to memorize. Only through repeated use did the connections between colors and objects become familiar. What had initially required a conscious effort to remember gradually became easier to recognize. The bags offered visible prompts for instructions I would otherwise have to look up. Written information on a phone screen became something I could recognize and act on in the kitchen. Seen as a means of communication, waste bags hold discarded items and convey their purpose through colors and markings. They turn abstract sorting requirements into information available at the moment of disposal. Their cues are simpler and more immediate than a webpage, while exceptions still require detailed guidance. The two complement each other: a visible cue helps with an ordinary decision, while the guide remains available when that cue alone is insufficient. On its sorting webpage, Brussels' public waste collection agency recommends downloading a sorting memo and displaying it somewhere visible, such as the refrigerator door. This small suggestion is revealing. Information's usefulness depends partly on when and where it appears. Seeing the relevant prompt while holding a piece of packaging removes one search between understanding and action. In Cognition in the Wild, cognitive anthropologist Edwin Hutchins examines how cognition unfolds through interactions among people, tools and their environment. This perspective helps me understand my sorting ability in context. Some knowledge is in my memory, some remains in the guide and some is prompted by colors and signs. Knowing how to sort includes knowing how to draw on these resources to make a decision. A Chinese student sorts glass bottles of different colors into the corresponding recycling bins on a street corner in Brussels, Belgium. Photo: Courtesy of Liu Collection schedules bring reminders into weekly routines Knowing which bag to use is only one step. Waste must also be put in the designated place at the right time. In Brussels, residents need to check when to put bags out according to their address; one street's schedule cannot be treated as the timetable for the whole city. For me, adapting to local life meant remembering the arrangements for my own address and fitting them into my weekly routine. By my third month, sorting had become more familiar, but I still sometimes forgot to put the bags out. One morning, as I was leaving home, I noticed bags outside my neighbors' doors and remembered the task I had missed. I felt inconvenienced and a little embarrassed. That feeling, however, did not mean my neighbors were judging me. What was clear was that their bags offered a timely, concrete reminder. This drew my attention to information conveyed without written notices. Actions already completed by others leave recognizable clues. Residents need not leave home together, or even speak, to carry out related tasks at different points in the week under the same collection arrangements. The days for putting bags out connect private kitchens with collection work on the street. This ordinary connection is easily overlooked, precisely because it is woven into such a routine domestic task. Communication research often asks whether a message is seen and understood. Habit formation raises another question: does a reminder reappear when action is needed? The guide explains, the timetable schedules the next task and the bags outside make that schedule visible. Conversations help everyday knowledge circulate Not everything I learned came from the web. My roommate provided the earliest reminders. Later, conversations with neighbors revealed how habits develop over time. One neighbor recalled putting all his waste in a single bag as a child. His recollection shifted my attention from his present ease to the gradual learning that had preceded it. The familiarity I saw in front of me had its own history. While visiting a colleague, I saw a drawing that her five-year-old daughter had brought home from kindergarten. It showed bins in different colors alongside the items belonging in each. In Dutch, she explained which "home" each object should go to. Sorting knowledge became something she wanted to share and could readily illustrate. I tried to make sense of her explanation across the language barrier, drawing on her gestures and what I already knew. As we communicated through gestures, I noticed that the drawing had found another use after traveling from kindergarten to home. Colors and pictures helped the child organize what she knew; explaining them brought her learning into a conversation at home. For that brief exchange, she was the one explaining and I, the adult visitor, the listener. Everyday knowledge does not always flow from older people to younger people. I also once received a rejection notice attached by a waste collector after I made a mistake with a waste bag. The experience made the gap between reading instructions and carrying them out clear. For someone still learning, whether feedback is easy to understand, and whether an explanation can be found when questions arise, directly affects the next attempt. From a roommate's reminder to a child's drawing and feedback at collection, sorting knowledge needs repeated explanation in specific situations. Elizabeth Shove, Mika Pantzar and Matt Watson identify materials, competences and meanings as three basic elements of social practice. Their approach examines how practices form and persist as connections between these elements are established, maintained and changed. In my experience, bags and collection facilities provide the material conditions; identifying and disposing of items requires skills acquired over time; keeping my surroundings clean and handling household waste responsibly give these actions everyday meaning. Communication helps connect these elements. Colors aid recognition, guides allow verification, conversations clarify doubts and schedules remind us of the next task. Environmental knowledge can thus become part of recurring activities. Yet reminders cannot replace convenient facilities and reliable collection services. Without them, even clear instructions may not enable people to sort their waste successfully. In assessing environmental communication, we should therefore ask more than how many people have encountered a campaign message. Are they less confused when disposing of a particular item? Do they know how to correct a mistake? Can the practice be sustained in daily life? My observations offer one way into these questions; they cannot represent the experiences of all Belgian households. From checking my phone with an object in hand to choosing the appropriate bag more naturally, I experienced a gradual process of familiarization. Kitchens, doorways and street corners were the settings for this learning. My roommate's reminders, a child's drawing and the bags outside neighbors' homes helped make life in an unfamiliar city something I could understand and participate in. When I think back to those rolls of colored bags, I think about how I gradually learned to live here. Perhaps a habit begins in such small, specific moments: information appears where it is needed, a question receives an answer, an action is completed and the action is remembered when the occasion arises again in everyday life. The author is Associate Professor at School of Television, Communication University of China

item.title: Mexico's crackdown on alleged Chinese steel transshipment to US lacks evidence and reflects Washington's pressure: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-12 23:49:00
An aerial view shows containers stacked on a cargo ship at the Port of Lázaro Cárdenas in Michoacán, Mexico, on April 25, 2025. Photo: VCG A Chinese expert warned on Thursday that tariffs imposed without evidence will only undermine Mexico's manufacturing competitiveness, and that establishing a relationship based on mutual respect and benefit is the only path toward sound China-Mexico trade ties. The comments came after Reuters reported that Mexico is working to block steel from China and other countries from being "rerouted" through Mexico into the US under North America's trade pact, a Mexican official said on Wednesday (local time). Luis Rosendo Gutierrez, Mexico's deputy economy minister for foreign trade, told journalists that the government has tightened traceability measures and the measures were preventing goods from reaching the US through misuse of Mexico's trade preferences. Gutierrez said that Mexico has canceled about 1,100 registrations for steel mills that authorities found did not exist, many of them in Asia, and that the move had helped cut steel imports from Vietnam by 80 percent over the past several months. Steel and aluminum imports from third countries - including China, South Korea and India - fell by about 30 percent, representing some 13 billion pesos ($698.54 million) in import value, the official said. Steel has become a politically sensitive flashpoint in US-Mexico trade, with Washington determined to block Chinese goods and inputs from entering the US market via third countries. The measures come as Mexico seeks relief from the US on steel, aluminum and vehicle tariffs, prioritizing it over a broader review of the US-Mexico-Canada trade pact. Zhou Mi, a senior researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the Global Times on Thursday that the so-called "transshipment" claims against Chinese steel products lack evidence, and that Mexico's targeting of Chinese steel is in fact being carried out under US pressure. The expert noted that Mexico should base any trade remedy measures on facts rather than act on another country's bidding, as blind protectionist measures will ultimately harm its own economic interests. Transshipment refers to goods being routed through a third country before reaching their final destination, typically to evade tariffs. The Reuters report cited analysts who argued that Mexico is not a hub for steel transshipment. Separately, a report last month by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank, claimed that certain goods may undergo significant processing in Mexico before being exported to the US, rather than simply passing through. Since 2025, Mexico has significantly ramped up trade protectionism against Chinese imports, launching multiple anti-dumping probes into Chinese products including float glass and PVC tarpaulins. In response, China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) launched an investigation in September last year pursuant to China's Foreign Trade Law and its rules on foreign trade barrier investigations. In March this year, the ministry released the final conclusions of a probe into Mexico's restrictions against China and other non-free trade agreement partners, stating that these measures constituted trade and investment barriers. The ministry is authorized to implement corresponding measures to resolutely safeguard the interests of Chinese industries, a ministry spokesperson said at the time. China is Mexico's second-largest trading partner, and Mexico is China's second-largest trading partner in Latin America. In the first nine months of 2026, bilateral trade continued to grow, rising 11.6 percent year-on-year to $92.05 billion, Chinese customs data showed. Zhou urged Mexicoto uphold its independence and make its own trade decisions in accord with international trade matters, rather than letting other countries determine its economic course. "Only by honoring its commitments to the international community while properly managing relations with all parties can Mexico achieve sustainable trade development and provide the necessary support for its national development," Zhou said. In response to Mexico's ramped-up protectionist measures, the Chinese government has on multiple occasions urged Mexico to reverse its erroneous unilateral tariff hikes, and voiced grave concern over Mexico's potential so-called "economic security review" targeting Chinese investment. China firmly opposes all forms of unilateralism and protectionism, and rejects the politicization, weaponization and instrumentalization of trade matters, a MOFCOM spokesperson said in March.

item.title: China approves first oral GLP-1 weight-loss drug
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-12 23:45:00
Photo: VCG China on Thursday approved Eli Lilly's orforglipron pills, marketed domestically under the brand name "Muyouda," for long-term weight management in adults, making it the country's first oral GLP-1 medication approved for weight loss, according to the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) and the company's press release on Thursday. According to the NMPA, the Class 1 innovative drug, submitted by Eli Lilly Nederland B.V., is intended for use alongside dietary changes and increased physical activity. It is approved for adults with an initial body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m² or above, or those with a BMI of at least 27 but below 30 kg/m² who have at least one weight-related condition, such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, high blood sugar, obstructive sleep apnea or cardiovascular disease. Orforglipron is an orally available, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist that is approved as a weight loss agent.It is a small molecule that binds to the GLP-1 receptor in the brain that regulates appetite and satiety. Engagement of the GLP-1 receptor results in a decrease in hunger and food intake leading to loss of excessive weight, according to National Library of Medicine website. China is among the first countries to approve the medication. Its indication for treating adults with type 2 diabetes is still under review by the NMPA, according to the company. The medication was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in April, 2026, under the brand name Foundayo for weight management, according to TIME magazine. Global Times

item.title: GT Voice: AI jitters in US raise stakes in China for S.Korea chip firms
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-12 23:43:00
Production of semiconductor chip File photo: VCG South Korea's semiconductor exports are booming, but a new cloud is gathering over the industry - and it comes from the US. In a report published on Thursday, the Financial Times, under the headline "AI jitters erupt after Democrats threaten data center build-out," warned that the construction boom could be brought to a standstill following the Democrats' victories in the US midterm elections. The political headwinds facing US data centers could spill over into South Korea's semiconductor industry, at least in part. In January, The Korea Herald cited analysts as saying that most memory products shipped by South Korean companies to the US, including high bandwidth memory (HBM) and server DRAM, are used in artificial intelligence (AI) servers and data centers. This leaves South Korean memory chipmakers exposed to any slowdown in US data center development, which could put some of the demand underpinning their exports at risk. The US is an important market for South Korean semiconductors, even if it is not the largest. In July, Chosun Biz cited data from the Bank of Korea showing that the US ranked fourth among destinations for South Korean semiconductor exports in 2025, with shipments worth $19.02 billion, up from $13.626 billion three years earlier. Its share of South Korea's total semiconductor exports also edged up, from 9.6 percent to 10.3 percent. The question now is whether political resistance to data center construction in the US could put the brakes on the growth of its semiconductor demand - or even cause it to stall or decline. For South Korean chipmakers, this is a development that warrants close attention, as well as a clear assessment of what it could mean for their export prospects. Whatever the eventual impact on US semiconductor demand, the AI jitters unleashed by the midterm elections may be enough to prompt South Korean chipmakers to think ahead. If they seek to diversify their markets against the risk of slower growth in US demand, China is likely to be high on their lists. The Chinese mainland remained the largest destination for South Korean semiconductor exports in 2025, taking shipments worth $74.46 billion, or 40.3 percent of the total. This comes as South Korea presses ahead with plans to expand its semiconductor capacity. The Yonhap News Agency reported in September that the country plans to double its semiconductor production capacity within five years. Yet with the outlook for US AI investment becoming less certain, South Korean chipmakers may have to look increasingly to non-US markets to sustain their export growth, further increasing the importance of the Chinese market. If South Korean chipmakers turn increasingly to China, they could intensify competition and put greater pressure on Chinese domestic memory producers. But the picture is more complicated. Memory chip prices remain high, with some segments poised for further increases, pointing to the strength of underlying demand and the potential of the Chinese market. One factor that South Korean chipmakers should not underestimate is the rapid technological progress of China's memory producers. Once they overcome the remaining technical hurdles, China's extensive industrial supply chains and manufacturing capacity could allow them to scale up production quickly, turning technological advances into a formidable competitive advantage. For South Korean chipmakers to maintain or expand their presence in China, they will need to offer Chinese customers their most advanced products. Finding a way to overcome US restrictions that prevent advanced HBM exports to China is therefore essential to that effort. That task may become harder. The controversy surrounding Jensen Huang, who has resigned as Nvidia's CEO, has fueled fresh calls in Washington for tighter restrictions on China's access to advanced chips. But with semiconductors so vital to South Korea's economy, its chipmakers have every reason to press for greater room to sell their most advanced products in China. It is a market where competition is intensifying, but whose importance to South Korean suppliers is also growing. South Korea should assert its own economic interests.

item.title: China's Mazu early weather warning box makes global debut
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-12 11:14:00
China intelligent meteorological solution MAZU is seen on display during the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai. Photo: VCG China's Mazu all-in-one box, an intelligent meteorological early warning solution, was officially launched globally at the COP31 High-Level Forum on South-South Cooperation on Climate Change in Antalya, Turkey, the China Meteorological Administration (CMA) said in a WeChat post on Thursday. MAZU, short for multi-hazard, alert, zero-gap and universal, is an AI-driven meteorological early warning platform named after the Chinese guardian goddess of the sea. The box is a lightweight, integrated hardware-software early warning solution designed to run the Mazu platform locally. It integrates storage, intelligent computing, networking, display and computation. Compatible with Ethernet, 5G and satellite communications, it delivers capabilities including nowcasting, an overview dashboard, operational monitoring and on-site AI assistance, enabling developing countries to rapidly ingest local observational data, according to the release. The box can run operations independently on site or connect to cloud resources and integrate with existing operational systems for coordinated operations. It supports modular expansion and continuous upgrading, helping local agencies strengthen their early warning operational capabilities, said the release. Given wide climatic variations worldwide, the CMA has worked closely with national meteorological and hydrological agencies to adapt Mazu into a weather tool tuned to local conditions. On November 1, China officially delivered a Mazu all-in-one box to Sri Lanka, which is expected to enter operational service by the end of 2026. It features custom-built modules for aviation, maritime and other sectors, aiming to help the Southern Asian country shore up its multi-hazard meteorological early-warning capabilities, CMA said. China delivered a customized version of its homegrown AI-powered meteorological early warning system to Nepal on September 22 to help the country improve early warning and disaster response. The move came after the CMA gave Nepal's meteorological department a version of Mazu for cloud-based trial use on August 29, following a deadly mudslide at the Gyirong-Rasuwa border crossing on the China-Nepal border, the Xinhua News Agency reported. As of October 2026, the Mazu solution had been deployed in eight countries, including Pakistan, Ethiopia and Sri Lanka, and tested through cloud-based trials in more than 50 countries, according to CMA. Global Times
